title: Spoken Language & Variation
description: How spoken English varies — accent, dialect, slang, sociolect and multi-modal language — and using that awareness to judge register in discussion, debate and speech delivery.

notes.heading: Accent vs Dialect
notes.body: Accent: HOW you pronounce words — the sounds, stress and pitch of your speech. In Somerset, 'bath' is often said with a long vowel; in Leeds, with a short one. Neither is right or wrong. Dialect: the WORDS and GRAMMAR a group uses — a group usually tied to a region or community. Vocabulary example: a bread roll is a 'barm' in Salford, a 'cob' in Nottingham, a 'bap' in Belfast, a 'batch' in Coventry and a 'roll' in London. Grammar example: 'I were' instead of 'I was' in parts of Yorkshire, or 'yous' as a plural 'you' in Liverpool and Glasgow. Even meals shift: in northern England 'dinner' can mean the midday meal and 'tea' the evening one. Key distinction to memorise: accent = pronunciation only; dialect = vocabulary + grammar. A common exam mistake is calling a dialect word an 'accent' — accents can't be written down, dialects can. Everyone has both an accent and a dialect; there is no 'accent-free' English.

notes.heading: Standard English and Formality
notes.body: Standard English: the widely accepted variety of English used in education, news reporting, official documents and most published writing. Crucially, Standard English is a dialect, not an accent — it can be spoken in any accent, from Glasgow to Cardiff to Newcastle. Received Pronunciation (RP), sometimes called 'BBC English', is just one accent associated with it, spoken by a small minority. Formality is a scale, not a switch: casual ('Hiya! You coming?'), informal/neutral ('Hi, are you coming?'), formal ('Good afternoon. Will you be attending?'). Standard English and formal register are expected in exams, job interviews, formal speeches and letters of complaint — contexts where you want to be judged on your ideas, not distracted from them. Common pitfall: thinking Standard English is 'better English'. It isn't superior linguistically; it's simply the agreed convention for formal, public communication — like wearing a uniform to an interview.

notes.heading: Slang and Sociolect
notes.body: Slang: very informal words and phrases used by particular groups, often deliberately different from Standard English. The word 'slang' has been around since 1756 and originally described the language of disreputable people — Dickens used it for the pickpockets in Oliver Twist, where 'green' meant innocent and 'covey' meant a friend. Slang works as a badge of identity: it signals who belongs to a group and who doesn't. It is often generational (your grandparents' slang is not yours), activity-based (gaming, sport and music all generate it) and sometimes localised — Cockney rhyming slang from 19th-century East London says 'apples and pears' for stairs and 'Uncle Ned' for bed. A sociolect is the broader term: the distinctive language variety of a social group. Slang dates fast — words like 'covey' die out while new ones appear — which is exactly why it works as a group marker. Rule of thumb: slang belongs in informal settings among people who share it. It sounds out of place from a newsreader, doctor or teacher — and in exams or formal speeches it costs you credibility.

notes.heading: Multi-modal Language
notes.body: Multi-modal communication: messages that combine several modes — words, images, emojis, punctuation, layout, even GIFs — to create meaning. Digital messaging has blurred the old line between speech and writing: a text message is written down, but it behaves like conversation — fast, informal, back-and-forth, full of spoken-style features (abbreviations, incomplete sentences, slang). Because text lacks the tone of voice, facial expressions and gestures of face-to-face talk, writers replace them: emojis and emoticons act as digital facial expressions, while exclamation marks, capitals and repeated letters ('soooo good!!!') carry emphasis and emotion. Language itself keeps evolving with technology — 'computer' named a person who did calculations in 1613, a calculating machine by 1869, and an electronic machine only from 1946. Exam skill: analysing how meaning is made when words alone would be ambiguous. 'Fine.' as a text reply can read as agreement or as fury — the full stop, the missing emoji and the context do the work.

notes.heading: Language, Identity and Attitudes
notes.body: Your accent and dialect carry clues about the places and people that shaped you — where you grew up, who raised you, the voices you heard. Variation is therefore tied to identity, and no variety of English is linguistically 'wrong': a Yorkshire dialect follows its own consistent grammar just as Standard English does. Yet people hold strong attitudes: listeners may (unfairly) judge a speaker's intelligence, trustworthiness or social class from accent alone. This is accent bias — a prejudice about people based on how they sound, not a fact about language. Writers exploit these attitudes deliberately: an author who gives a character dialect ('I dunno, do I?') rather than Standard English is characterising — signalling region, class, age or attitude in a single line of dialogue. When you analyse fiction, ask what a character's variety tells us and why the writer chose it. When you analyse real speech, catch yourself judging the speaker rather than the ideas — in a debate or discussion, an unfamiliar accent tells you nothing about the quality of an argument.

notes.heading: Register: Matching Language to Context
notes.body: Register: the level of formality and style you choose for a particular audience, purpose and setting. Skilled speakers shift register constantly — the same person says 'Mate, that lesson dragged' at break and 'I found that lesson challenging' in a parent meeting. This shifting is called code-switching, and everyone does it; it is a social skill, not dishonesty. To judge register, ask three questions: WHO is my audience (friends, teachers, strangers, examiners)? WHAT is my purpose (persuade, inform, entertain, complain)? WHERE is this happening (corridor, classroom, interview, public speech)? Register is mismatched when the answers don't align with the language: slang in a formal speech undermines authority, but stiff formality with friends can sound cold or mocking. Common pitfall: assuming formal = always better. Over-formality in a casual context is as much a mismatch as slang in a formal one. The goal is appropriateness — language that fits the situation so listeners focus on your message.

notes.heading: Applying Variation Awareness When You Speak
notes.body: Everything in this topic becomes practical when you speak in public. In a formal speech, debate or assessed discussion, lean towards Standard English and a formal-to-neutral register: it keeps attention on your argument and signals respect for the audience — but you don't need to change your accent, only your word and grammar choices. Used deliberately and sparingly, informal features can be a weapon: a well-timed colloquial phrase or touch of humour builds rapport and makes a point memorable, as long as it suits the audience. In discussion and debate, variation awareness cuts both ways: choose your own register consciously, and judge others on their arguments, never on their accent or dialect — dismissing an idea because of how someone sounds is both unfair and a weak move (it's close to attacking the person, not the argument). This builds directly on eng-speaking-1 (presentations, discussion and listening) and eng-persuasive-speaking-1 (rhetoric and argument structure): those topics teach you HOW to deliver and structure speech; this one teaches you WHICH variety of English to deliver it in.

flashcards.definition: How a person pronounces words — the sounds, stress and pitch of their speech. Pronunciation only, not word choice.
flashcards.example: Saying 'bath' with a long vowel in Somerset vs a short vowel in Leeds.

flashcards.definition: The vocabulary and grammar used by a group of people, usually from a particular region or community.
flashcards.example: A bread roll called a 'barm', 'cob', 'bap' or 'batch' depending on where you are in the UK.

flashcards.definition: The widely accepted variety of English used in education, news, official documents and formal writing. A dialect, not an accent.
flashcards.example: 'We were walking' (Standard) vs 'We was walking' (non-standard dialect grammar).

flashcards.definition: An accent traditionally associated with Standard English and the BBC, spoken by a small minority — not required to speak Standard English.
flashcards.example: Standard English can be spoken perfectly well in a Glasgow or Cardiff accent; RP is just one accent.

flashcards.definition: Very informal words used by particular groups, often generational or activity-based, signalling group identity.
flashcards.example: Words you use with friends that you would never use with a teacher or in a shop.

flashcards.definition: The distinctive language variety of a social group — defined by age, interests, occupation or community rather than region.
flashcards.example: Gaming slang, football-terrace vocabulary, or the shared terms used within a friendship group.

flashcards.definition: An informal, everyday word or phrase used in casual conversation — milder and more widely understood than slang.
flashcards.example: 'Gonna', 'a bit of a nightmare', 'no worries' — informal but not tied to one tight group.

flashcards.definition: The level of formality and style chosen to suit audience, purpose and setting.
flashcards.example: Casual: 'Hiya! You coming?' Formal: 'Good afternoon. Will you be attending?'

flashcards.definition: Shifting between language varieties or registers depending on who you are speaking to and where.
flashcards.example: Using slang with friends at break, then Standard English when answering the headteacher.

flashcards.definition: Communication combining several modes — words, images, emojis, punctuation, layout — to create meaning.
flashcards.example: 'soooo good!!! 😄' — repeated letters, exclamation marks and emoji carry the emotion words alone can't.

flashcards.definition: A localised slang where a phrase rhymes with the intended word; originated in 19th-century East London (Cockney).
Judging a person's intelligence, class or trustworthiness from how they sound — a prejudice, not a fact about language.
flashcards.example: Assuming a speaker with a strong regional accent is less clever — unfair, and says nothing about their argument.

choices: The words and grammar a group of people use
How a person pronounces words — sounds, stress and pitch
The level of formality someone chooses
Informal words used by a particular group
questions.explanation: Accent covers pronunciation only — the sounds, stress and pitch of speech. Words and grammar belong to dialect, formality is register, and informal group words are slang.

questions.stem: A dialect differs from an accent because a dialect includes:
choices: Vocabulary and grammar
Only pronunciation
Only spelling
Body language and gesture
questions.explanation: Dialect = the words and grammar a group uses (e.g. 'cob' for a bread roll, 'I were' for 'I was'). Pronunciation alone is accent — that's the distinction examiners test most often.

choices: Grammatically incorrect English
The formal language of official documents
Very informal words used by particular groups, often marking identity
Any word borrowed from another language
questions.explanation: Slang is informal group language — generational, activity-based or localised — that signals who belongs. It isn't 'incorrect'; it follows its own conventions and is simply wrong for formal contexts.

choices: The widely accepted variety used in education, news and official documents
English spoken with Received Pronunciation
The oldest and most correct form of English
The way everyone in southern England speaks
questions.explanation: Standard English is the agreed variety for formal, public communication — a dialect, not an accent. It can be spoken in any accent, and it isn't linguistically 'better', just the convention for exams and formal settings.

questions.stem: 'Running late, be there in 10 🚌😅' — this message is an example of:
choices: Formal register
Standard English
A regional dialect
Multi-modal language
questions.explanation: The message combines words with emojis to create meaning — the defining feature of multi-modal language. Digital messages blend writing with speech-like informality, using emojis and punctuation to carry tone.

questions.stem: 'We was walking to the shop.' This sentence is best described as an example of:
choices: Slang
An accent
Non-standard dialect grammar
Multi-modal language
questions.explanation: The variation is in grammar ('we was' vs standard 'we were'), so it's dialect, not slang (which is vocabulary) or accent (which is pronunciation and can't be written down). It's a consistent feature of some dialects — not a mistake the speaker needs 'correcting' in informal contexts.

questions.stem: In which situation would slang be most appropriate?
choices: Chatting with friends at lunchtime
A job interview
A formal speech to the school governors
A letter of complaint to a company
questions.explanation: Slang fits informal settings among people who share it. In interviews, formal speeches and complaint letters it undermines credibility — the audience expects Standard English and a more formal register.

questions.stem: A student uses slang with friends in the corridor, then switches to Standard English when presenting to the class. This is called:
choices: Accent bias
Code-switching
Rhyming slang
Colloquialism
questions.explanation: Code-switching is shifting between varieties or registers to suit audience, purpose and setting — a normal social skill everyone uses, not dishonesty. Accent bias is judging people by how they sound; rhyming slang is a specific slang type.

questions.stem: Why do texters use emojis, exclamation marks and repeated letters ('soooo good!!!')?
choices: Because they cannot spell correctly
To replace the tone of voice, facial expressions and gestures missing from written text
Because it is required by messaging apps
To make the message more formal
questions.explanation: Text lacks the paralinguistic cues of face-to-face talk, so writers substitute them digitally: emojis act as facial expressions, while punctuation and stretched spelling carry emphasis and emotion. It's a deliberate meaning-making choice, not poor spelling.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the wrong register for a formal presentation to the school governors?
choices: 'The data shows a clear improvement in attendance.'
'I'd like to draw your attention to the results.'
'Honestly, the old system was a total shambles, mate.'
'Thank you for the opportunity to speak today.'
questions.explanation: 'Total shambles' and 'mate' are informal/colloquial — mismatched with a formal audience and purpose. The other options use Standard English and a suitably formal register. Register is judged by audience, purpose and setting together.

questions.stem: Why do social groups develop their own slang and sociolect?
choices: Because they don't know Standard English
To confuse teachers and parents deliberately
To signal identity and belonging — marking who is inside the group
Because slang is easier to spell
questions.explanation: Group language works as a badge of identity: shared words signal membership and exclude outsiders. Slang changes fast precisely because it must stay distinctive — once everyone uses a word, the group moves on.

questions.stem: In a debate, an opponent argues well but speaks with a strong regional accent. Which response shows good variation awareness?
choices: Pointing out the accent to weaken their credibility with the audience
Judging the argument on its evidence and reasoning, since accent says nothing about its quality
Assuming their argument is less informed because of how they sound
Asking them to repeat themselves in Standard English
questions.explanation: Attacking or discounting someone because of their accent is accent bias — and it's also close to attacking the person rather than the argument, a weak move in debate. Strong debaters engage with evidence and reasoning; Standard English can be spoken in any accent anyway.

questions.stem: In northern England 'dinner' often means the midday meal and 'tea' the evening one; in southern England 'dinner' is the evening meal. Which statement is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: The northern usage is incorrect because it confuses two meals
The southern usage is Standard English, so the north should adopt it
Both are valid dialect vocabulary — regional variation where neither is right or wrong
These are slang terms that should only be used among friends
questions.explanation: This is lexical (vocabulary) variation between regional dialects, and no dialect is linguistically 'wrong'. It isn't slang — these are established regional words, not informal group markers — and Standard English doesn't settle which meal-name is correct.

questions.stem: A friend replies to your long message with just 'Fine.' and you worry they're angry. Why is a text like this so easy to misread?
choices: Because 'fine' is always an angry word
Because text lacks tone of voice and facial expression, so tiny cues like a full stop or missing emoji carry extra weight
Because Standard English is ambiguous
Because your friend is code-switching
questions.explanation: Written messages strip out the paralinguistic cues (tone, expression, gesture) that clarify meaning face-to-face, so readers over-interpret small signals — punctuation, length, missing emojis. Analysing that ambiguity is the core multi-modal skill.

questions.stem: Which statement about Standard English and accent is most accurate?
choices: Standard English can only be spoken with Received Pronunciation
Standard English is an accent as well as a dialect
Standard English is a dialect that can be spoken in any accent
People with regional accents cannot use Standard English
questions.explanation: Standard English is defined by vocabulary and grammar — a dialect — so it can be pronounced in any accent, from Glasgow to Cardiff. RP is just one accent traditionally associated with it, spoken by a small minority. This fine accent/dialect distinction is the classic exam trap.
